summary: This standards-track document defines a YANG data model for managing IP on a device, including configuration and state. It follows the Network Management Datastore Architecture described in RFC 8342. It obsoletes RFC 7277.

eli5.summary: Every device has an address like a house number. This is a standard form for setting and viewing those numbers in a way all makers understand.

subtitle: A YANG model for configuring and monitoring IPv4 and IPv6 settings on each network interface.

tldr.problem: Operators need a common way to configure per-interface IPv4 and IPv6 parameters, address lists and address-to-link-layer mappings, and to see which are actually in use.
tldr.mechanism: The ietf-ip YANG module augments each interface from RFC 8343 with ipv4 and ipv6 containers holding enable and forwarding switches, MTU, address lists, neighbor lists and IPv6 autoconfiguration settings.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 7277 by moving all read-only data under /interfaces/interface to fit the Network Management Datastore Architecture.

today: RFC 8344 is a Proposed Standard and replaces RFC 7277. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it augments the interface model of RFC 8343.

sections.title: What the IP Model Covers
sections.content:
RFC 8344 defines a YANG data model for managing IP implementations. It covers configuration of per-interface IPv4 and IPv6 parameters and mappings of IP addresses to link-layer addresses. It also reports which IP addresses are operationally used and which link-layer mappings exist.

The per-interface parameters are added by augmenting the interface model from RFC 8343. The model supports the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) from RFC 8342.

It obsoletes RFC 7277. The ipv4 and ipv6 subtrees under /interfaces-state/interface are deprecated, and all config false nodes are now in the subtrees under /interfaces/interface. Servers MAY still implement the deprecated subtrees for clients that do not support NMDA.
sections.eli5: This form adds the address boxes to each plug-in point's entry, so you can write down and read back its numbers.

sections.title: The ipv4 and ipv6 Containers
sections.content:
The module ietf-ip augments each interface with two containers, ipv4 and ipv6. In each, the enabled leaf controls whether that address family is on for the interface, and forwarding controls whether IP packet forwarding is enabled for it. Each container also has a list of addresses and a list of IP-to-link-layer mappings.

Both containers are presence containers, and IP is enabled unless enabled (which defaults to true) is set to false. Forwarding defaults to false. If an interface cannot run IP, the server must not allow these parameters to be configured.

Each family also has an mtu leaf, the size in octets of the largest IP packet the interface will send and receive. The IPv4 range starts at 68 and the IPv6 range starts at 1280. If it is not configured, the MTU actually used depends on the interface type.
sections.eli5: Each plug-in point gets two small forms, one for the old kind of address and one for the new kind, each with an on/off switch and a packet-size limit.

sections.title: Addresses and Neighbor Entries
sections.content:
Each address list entry is keyed by ip. For IPv4 the subnet is a prefix-length (0 to 32) or, if the server supports the ipv4-non-contiguous-netmasks feature, a netmask. For IPv6 a prefix-length (0 to 128) is mandatory.

A read-only origin says where an address came from: other, static, dhcp, link-layer (IPv6 autoconfiguration that embeds a link-layer address) or random (for example a temporary address from RFC 4941 or an opaque one from RFC 7217). IPv6 addresses also have a read-only status such as preferred, deprecated, tentative, duplicate or optimistic.

The neighbor list maps an IP address to a mandatory link-layer-address. In the intended configuration its entries are static entries in the ARP cache (IPv4) or Neighbor Cache (IPv6). In the operational state the list represents that cache, and each entry's origin is other, static or dynamic, the last meaning resolved by ARP or IPv6 Neighbor Discovery.
sections.eli5: Each plug-in point has a list of its house numbers and a little address book of neighbors. The form also notes how each number was obtained.

sections.title: IPv6 Neighbor State and Autoconfiguration
sections.content:
IPv6 neighbor entries add read-only is-router and state leaves. The state values are incomplete, reachable, stale, delay and probe, which follow Neighbor Unreachability Detection in RFC 4861.

The dup-addr-detect-transmits leaf (default 1) sets how many consecutive Neighbor Solicitation messages are sent for Duplicate Address Detection on a tentative address. Zero means detection is not performed.

The autoconf container controls address autoconfiguration as described in RFC 4862. create-global-addresses defaults to true. With the ipv6-privacy-autoconf feature, create-temporary-addresses (default false) turns on temporary addresses, along with valid and preferred lifetime leaves.
sections.eli5: For the new kind of address, the form also tracks whether each neighbor was seen recently, and how many times to shout "is anyone else using this number?" before using it.

sections.title: Relationship to the IP-MIB
sections.content:
If a device implements the IP-MIB from RFC 4293, each entry in the ipv4/address and ipv6/address lists maps to one ipAddressEntry, and entries in the neighbor lists map to ipNetToPhysicalTable.

The RFC includes a table of the mappings. For example ipv4/enabled maps to ipv4InterfaceEnableStatus, ipv6/forwarding to ipv6InterfaceForwarding, ipv6/address/status to ipAddressStatus and ipv6/neighbor/state to ipNetToPhysicalState.

The IP-MIB's objects for IPv6 Router Advertisement are not here. The corresponding YANG nodes are defined in RFC 8022.
sections.eli5: Older tools used another form for the same facts. A table says which box on the new form matches which box on the old one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As in RFC 8343, the module is meant to be reached over NETCONF or RESTCONF. SSH is the mandatory-to-implement secure transport for NETCONF and TLS for RESTCONF, and the access control model in RFC 8341 can restrict users.

The RFC lists writable nodes that are sensitive. Changing enabled can open an unsecured path into a node or push traffic elsewhere. Changing addresses can make a node ignore messages meant for it or accept ones it would otherwise ignore. Changing forwarding can deny service or open a conduit into an area. Changing ipv6/autoconf can indirectly affect user privacy. Very small mtu values can slow down interfaces.
sections.eli5: If someone sneaks in and changes the numbers or switches on the form, the device could stop hearing its mail or let in the wrong visitors.
